subtopics.title: Drawing Sheets, Dimensioning, Scales & Line Diagrams
subtopics.subtitle: Sheet sizes and layout, line types, lettering, dimensioning, scales and line diagrams

concepts.text: Engineering drawings are prepared on standard ISO A-series sheets so that they can be printed, filed and exchanged without confusion. A0 has an area of one square metre and every sheet has sides in the ratio 1 : sqrt(2); halving the longer side of one size gives the next smaller size. Indian standard SP 46 (followed in Nepal) and ISO 5457 describe the sheet layout: a border line, a wider filing margin on the left, a title block, and optional grid references and fold marks.
Main elements of a drawing sheet layout:
items: Borders and frame: a thick border line encloses the drawing space; the left margin is wider to allow binding or filing.

Title block: placed at the bottom right-hand corner so it stays visible when the sheet is folded; it records drawing title, drawing number, scale, projection symbol, material, name of the organisation, drawn/checked/approved by and dates.
Revision table and parts list (bill of materials) are placed near or above the title block on assembly drawings.
Lettering is single-stroke, uppercase, vertical or inclined at 75 degrees; common heights are 3.5, 5, 7 and 10 mm, with larger heights used for titles and drawing numbers.

rows: Dimension, extension, leader and hatching lines
Centre lines, axes, pitch circles, lines of symmetry
Thin chain, thick at ends and at changes of direction
Short or long break lines, limits of partial views

items: Every feature is dimensioned once only, in the view that shows its shape most clearly; redundant dimensions are avoided.
Dimensions are placed outside the view where possible, smaller dimensions nearer the view and larger ones further out so that extension lines do not cross dimension lines.
Hidden lines should not be dimensioned; centre lines and outlines must never be used as dimension lines.
All dimensions are normally in millimetres, stated once by a note (e.g. ALL DIMENSIONS IN mm) instead of writing units on every figure.
Arrowheads are filled, with length about three times their width; extension lines start just clear of the outline and extend slightly beyond the dimension line.

rows: Figures placed parallel to the dimension line, readable from the bottom or right-hand side
All figures read from the bottom edge of the sheet; dimension lines broken for the figure
Dimensions placed end to end; tolerances accumulate
All dimensions measured from a common datum; no accumulation of error
Chain and parallel dimensioning used together on one drawing

concepts.text: A scale is the ratio of a length on the drawing to the corresponding actual length of the object. Full scale is 1 : 1; reduced scales such as 1 : 2, 1 : 5, 1 : 10, 1 : 100 are used for large objects such as buildings and maps; enlarged scales such as 2 : 1, 5 : 1, 10 : 1 are used for small parts like watch components. The representative fraction (RF) expresses the scale as a pure number with both lengths in the same unit. Example: a 20 m long hall drawn 50 cm long has RF = 50 / 2000 = 1/40.

concepts.latex: RF = \frac{\text{length on drawing}}{\text{actual length}},\quad L_{scale} = RF \times L_{max}
concepts.plainText: RF = drawing length / actual length (same units); length of scale = RF x maximum length to be measured

concepts.text:
Worked example: diagonal scale, RF = 1/4000, to read metres up to 500 m
Length of scale = 500 m x 1/4000 = 50000 cm / 4000 = 12.5 cm
Main divisions: 5 parts of 2.5 cm, each = 100 m
First main division subdivided into 10 parts, each = 10 m
Diagonal: 10 equal horizontal divisions on the vertical, each step = 1 m
Reading 356 m: 3 main divisions + 5 sub-divisions + 6th horizontal line

items: Plain scale: shows two units (e.g. metres and decimetres, or km and hm), or one unit and its fraction.
Diagonal scale: shows three successive units (e.g. m, dm, cm) using the property of similar triangles along a diagonal.
Vernier scale: also reads to a third unit using a primary scale and a sliding or fixed vernier; the least count equals the difference between one main-scale and one vernier-scale division.
Scale of chords: used for setting out or measuring angles when a protractor is not available.

concepts.text: A line diagram represents a system, structure or process by simple lines and standard symbols instead of a full-size pictorial drawing. Examples are frame diagrams of trusses, piping and flow diagrams, block diagrams of control systems, network topology diagrams, and building plans drawn with single lines for walls. In electrical engineering a single-line (one-line) diagram shows a three-phase power system by a single line per circuit, with standard symbols for generators, transformers, breakers, buses and loads. Line diagrams communicate the arrangement and connections rather than the exact shape and dimensions.

formulas.plainText: RF = length on drawing / actual length (same units)
Length of scale = RF x maximum length to be measured
Area of sheet An = 2^(-n) square metres

notes.text: When computing an RF, always convert both lengths to the same unit first: 1 cm representing 5 m means 1 cm : 500 cm, so RF = 1/500.
A plain scale reads two units, while diagonal and vernier scales read three units; choose a diagonal scale when a reading to the third unit is required.
Do not mix up line types: hidden edges use thin dashed lines, centre lines use thin chain lines, and cutting planes use thin chain lines with thick ends.

formulas.title: Representative fraction
formulas.plainText: RF = length on drawing / actual length
formulas.description: Scale expressed as a pure ratio with both lengths in the same unit.

formulas.title: Length of scale
formulas.plainText: Length of scale = RF x maximum length
formulas.description: Length to draw a plain or diagonal scale that must measure up to a given maximum length.

formulas.title: A-series sheet area
formulas.description: Each A-series size has half the area of the previous one, starting from 1 m^2 for A0.

flashcards.front: What are the dimensions of A0 and A4 drawing sheets?
flashcards.back: A0 is 841 x 1189 mm (area 1 m^2) and A4 is 210 x 297 mm.

flashcards.front: Difference between aligned and unidirectional dimensioning?
flashcards.back: Aligned figures are parallel to the dimension line and read from the bottom or right; unidirectional figures all read from the bottom of the sheet.

flashcards.front: How many units can a diagonal scale read?
flashcards.back: Three successive units, for example metres, decimetres and centimetres.
A simplified diagram of a three-phase power system showing each circuit by one line with standard symbols for equipment.

questions.questionText: The size of an A3 drawing sheet is:
questions.explanation: A3 is half of A2 (420 x 594 mm), giving 297 x 420 mm.

questions.questionText: On a drawing, 1 cm represents 5 m. The representative fraction is:
A plain scale of RF 1/50000 is to measure distances up to 5 km. The length of the scale is:
Which line type is used to show hidden edges of an object?
questions.explanation: Hidden outlines and edges are drawn with thin dashed lines; thin chain lines are for centre lines.

questions.questionText: In which dimensioning method are all dimensions measured from a common reference so that errors do not accumulate?
questions.explanation: Parallel or datum dimensioning measures every feature from one datum, avoiding the cumulative error of chain dimensioning.

subtopics.title: Orthographic Projection: First- & Third-Angle Views
subtopics.subtitle: Planes and quadrants, first- vs third-angle layout, points, lines and multi-view drawing

concepts.text: Orthographic projection represents a three-dimensional object by two or more two-dimensional views, each obtained by projectors drawn perpendicular to a plane of projection. The observer is imagined at infinity, so projectors are parallel and every view shows true dimensions of surfaces parallel to that plane. It is the standard method for manufacturing and construction drawings because sizes can be measured directly.

items: Vertical plane (VP): receives the front view (elevation), showing length and height.
Horizontal plane (HP): receives the top view (plan), showing length and width.
Profile plane (PP): perpendicular to both, receives the side view (end view), showing width and height.
The line of intersection of HP and VP is the reference line XY; after projection the HP is rotated to lie in the plane of the VP.

concepts.text: The HP and VP intersect to form four quadrants (dihedral angles). Placing the object in the first quadrant gives first-angle projection; placing it in the third quadrant gives third-angle projection. Second- and fourth-angle projections are not used because after rotating the HP the front and top views overlap on the same side of XY.

rows: On the right of front view
On the left of front view
India (BIS SP 46), Nepal, Europe (ISO method E)

concepts.text: The method of projection is indicated in the title block by a symbol showing the front view and left side view of a truncated cone. In the first-angle symbol the circles (end view) appear to the right of the trapezium; in the third-angle symbol they appear to the left.

items: A point h above HP and d in front of VP: front view is h above XY and top view is d below XY, both on one projector perpendicular to XY.
A point lying in the VP has its top view on XY; a point lying in the HP has its front view on XY.
In third-angle projection the top view lies above XY and the front view below XY.
A line parallel to a plane shows its true length on that plane.
A line perpendicular to HP appears as a point in the top view and in true length in the front view.
A line inclined to both planes appears shortened in both views; its true length is found by rotation or an auxiliary plane.

concepts.plainText: True length = sqrt(top view length^2 + (difference of end heights above HP)^2)

items: Choose as front view the side that shows the most characteristic shape and the fewest hidden lines.
Use the minimum number of views that fully describe the object: a cylinder or sphere-like part may need only two, most parts need three.
Views must be aligned on common projectors: front and top share length, front and side share height, top and side share width.
Hidden features are shown with thin dashed lines; axes of holes and symmetry with thin chain lines.

concepts.text:
Layout on sheet (first-angle):
           [ FRONT VIEW ]   [ LEFT SIDE VIEW ]
  --------------------------------------  XY
           [ TOP VIEW   ]
Layout on sheet (third-angle):
           [ TOP VIEW   ]
           [ FRONT VIEW ]   [ RIGHT SIDE VIEW ]

formulas.plainText: True length = sqrt(top view length^2 + (h2 - h1)^2)
Top view length = TL cos(theta), front view length = TL cos(phi); theta, phi = inclinations to HP and VP

notes.text: Remember the first-angle rule: what you see from above is drawn below, and what you see from the left is drawn on the right.
Nepal follows Indian and ISO practice, so first-angle projection is the default on drawings and in examinations unless stated otherwise.
Second and fourth quadrants are not used for drawings because the front and top views overlap after the HP is rotated.

formulas.title: True length of a line
formulas.description: True length from the top-view length and the difference in heights of the two ends above HP.

formulas.title: Foreshortened projections
formulas.plainText: Ltop = TL cos(theta), Lfront = TL cos(phi)
formulas.description: Projected lengths of a line inclined at theta to HP and phi to VP.

flashcards.front: In first-angle projection, where is the top view placed?
Which angle of projection is used in the USA?
flashcards.back: Third-angle projection, where the plane lies between observer and object and the top view is drawn above the front view.

flashcards.front: How does a line perpendicular to HP appear in the top view?
flashcards.back: As a point; its front view shows its true length.

questions.questionText: In first-angle projection, the top view of an object is drawn:
options: To the left of the front view
To the right of the front view
questions.explanation: In first-angle projection the HP is rotated downward, so the plan appears below the elevation.

questions.questionText: In third-angle projection the object is placed in the third quadrant, which means:
options: The plane of projection lies between the observer and the object
The object lies between the observer and the plane
The object lies in the plane of projection
The observer is at a finite distance
questions.explanation: In third-angle projection the planes are imagined transparent and lie between the observer and the object.

questions.questionText: A point P is 20 mm above HP and 30 mm in front of VP. In first-angle projection its front and top views are respectively:
options: 30 mm above XY and 20 mm below XY
20 mm below XY and 30 mm above XY
20 mm above XY and 30 mm above XY
20 mm above XY and 30 mm below XY
questions.explanation: The front view shows height above HP (20 mm above XY); the top view shows distance in front of VP, drawn 30 mm below XY.

questions.questionText: The top view of a line is 40 mm long. Its ends are 10 mm and 40 mm above HP. Its true length is:
Why are second- and fourth-angle projections not used in engineering drawing?
options: The front and top views overlap after rotation of HP
questions.explanation: In the second and fourth quadrants both views fall on the same side of XY and overlap, making the drawing confusing.

subtopics.title: Isometric Projection & Pictorial Views
subtopics.subtitle: Axonometric family, isometric scale, isometric view vs projection, oblique and perspective

concepts.text: A pictorial drawing shows the length, width and height of an object in a single view, so it is easy to understand even for non-specialists. The main families are axonometric projection (isometric, dimetric, trimetric), oblique projection and perspective projection. Pictorial views support orthographic drawings in catalogues, assembly instructions, sketches and presentations, but they are rarely used alone for manufacture because many lengths and angles are distorted.

In isometric projection the object is tilted so that its three principal edges make equal angles with the plane of projection. The three isometric axes appear 120 degrees apart: one vertical and two at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Lines parallel to these axes are isometric lines and are all foreshortened in the same ratio; lines not parallel to the axes (non-isometric lines) cannot be measured directly and are located by their end points.

concepts.plainText: Isometric length / true length = cos45 / cos30 = sqrt(2/3) = 0.816

concepts.text:
Worked example: isometric projection of a 50 mm cube
Isometric length = 0.816 x 50 = 40.8 mm on each of the three axes
Isometric view (true lengths) would draw each edge 50 mm
Ratio view / projection = 1 / 0.816 = 1.225, i.e. view about 22.5% larger
Isometric scale construction: true scale at 45 degrees, isometric scale at 30 degrees,
verticals dropped from true divisions give isometric divisions

items: Isometric projection: drawn with the isometric scale, so all isometric lines are 0.816 of true length.
Isometric view (isometric drawing): drawn with true lengths along the axes; same shape, but about 22.5% larger.
The isometric view is more common in practice because it saves drawing an isometric scale.
Circles on isometric faces appear as ellipses, usually drawn by the four-centre method or the box (offset) method.

concepts.text: In oblique projection the front face is drawn parallel to the picture plane in true shape and size, and the receding edges are drawn at an angle, usually 30, 45 or 60 degrees. It is convenient for objects with circles or irregular outlines on one face, since those are drawn in true shape.

Perspective projection shows an object as the eye sees it from a finite station point: projectors converge to the eye, so parallel receding lines meet at vanishing points and distant parts appear smaller. One-point (parallel), two-point (angular) and three-point (oblique) perspectives are distinguished by the number of vanishing points. It gives the most realistic image and is used by architects and in presentations, but it is not used for measurement.
When to use each pictorial method:
items: Isometric: technical illustration, piping isometrics, assembly sketches where all three faces matter equally.
Oblique: objects with a characteristic front face containing circles or curves.
Perspective: architectural renderings and presentations where realism matters more than measurement.
Orthographic: manufacturing and construction drawings where exact dimensions are required.

notes.text: If a question says isometric projection, multiply true lengths by 0.816; if it says isometric view or isometric drawing, use true lengths.
Cavalier oblique uses full scale on the receding axis and cabinet oblique uses half scale.
Only isometric lines can be measured directly; locate non-isometric lines and curves by plotting their end points or offsets.

formulas.title: Isometric scale
formulas.description: Foreshortening factor applied to every isometric line in an isometric projection.

formulas.title: View to projection ratio
formulas.description: An isometric view drawn with true lengths is about 22.5% larger than the isometric projection.

flashcards.front: What is the angle between isometric axes?
flashcards.back: 120 degrees; one axis is vertical and the other two are at 30 degrees to the horizontal.

flashcards.front: How does a circle appear on an isometric face?
flashcards.back: As an ellipse, commonly drawn by the four-centre method.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes perspective from parallel projections?
flashcards.back: Its projectors converge to a finite station point, so receding parallel lines meet at vanishing points.

questions.questionText: The edges of a 60 mm cube are drawn in isometric projection. The length of each edge on the drawing is approximately:
questions.explanation: Isometric length = 0.816 x 60 = 48.99, about 49 mm.

questions.questionText: The angle between any two isometric axes is:
questions.explanation: The three isometric axes are equally spaced at 120 degrees.

questions.questionText: In cabinet oblique projection, lengths along the receding axis are drawn to:
questions.explanation: Cabinet oblique halves the receding lengths; cavalier oblique uses full scale.

questions.questionText: Compared with the isometric projection of the same object, an isometric view (drawing) is:
questions.explanation: The isometric view uses true lengths, so it is 1/0.816, about 1.225 times, the size of the isometric projection.

questions.questionText: In which pictorial method do receding parallel lines converge to vanishing points?
questions.explanation: Perspective uses projectors converging to the eye, so parallel lines meet at vanishing points; the other methods use parallel projectors.

subtopics.title: Sectional Drawings
subtopics.subtitle: Cutting planes, hatching, types of sections and items not sectioned

concepts.text: When an object has complicated interior details, ordinary views are cluttered with hidden lines that are hard to read. A sectional view imagines the object cut by a cutting plane, with the portion nearer the observer removed, so that the interior is shown with visible lines. The cut surface is hatched to distinguish solid material from empty space.

items: The cutting plane is shown in an adjacent view by a thin chain line, thick at the ends and at changes of direction, with arrows showing the direction of viewing and letters such as A-A.
Section lines (hatching) are thin continuous lines, usually at 45 degrees to the main outline or axis, evenly spaced (commonly 1 to 2 mm apart, more for large areas).
Adjacent parts in an assembly are hatched in opposite directions or with different spacing; the same part is hatched identically in all views.
Hidden lines are normally omitted in sectional views unless essential for clarity.
Thin sections such as gaskets and sheet metal may be shown entirely filled (solid black).

rows: Plane passes completely through the object
One quarter removed; half shows interior, half exterior
Cutting plane stepped to pass through off-line features
Cross-section rotated 90 degrees in place on the view
Cross-section drawn outside the view, labelled
Small portion broken out by a freehand line
Features rotated into the cutting plane

concepts.text: In a half section of a symmetrical object, a centre line (not a thick line) separates the sectioned half from the unsectioned half, and hidden lines are omitted from the unsectioned half. An offset section is drawn as if the cutting plane were flat; the changes of direction are not shown as lines in the sectional view.

Certain parts are not hatched when the cutting plane passes along their length, because a section would give a false impression of their shape and add no information. They are shown in outside view even though the plane passes through them; they may be hatched when cut across their axis.
Items normally shown unsectioned when cut longitudinally:
items: Shafts, spindles, pins, keys and cotters.
Bolts, nuts, screws, studs, rivets and washers.
Ribs, webs, spokes of wheels and teeth of gears.
Balls and rollers of bearings.

concepts.text: When a solid is cut by a plane inclined to the reference planes, the section appears foreshortened in the ordinary views. Its true shape is obtained on an auxiliary plane parallel to the cutting plane. For a vertical cylinder cut by a plane inclined at angle theta to HP, the true section is an ellipse whose minor axis equals the diameter and whose major axis is D / cos theta.

concepts.plainText: Major axis = D / cos(theta), minor axis = D (vertical cylinder, plane at theta to HP)

concepts.text:
Worked example: vertical cylinder D = 40 mm cut by a plane at 45 degrees to HP
Minor axis of true section = D = 40 mm
Major axis = 40 / cos 45 = 40 / 0.7071 = 56.6 mm
Top view of the section = circle of 40 mm (coincides with the cylinder plan)

items: Show the cutting-plane line in the view where it appears as an edge, and label the section view (SECTION A-A).
Choose the cutting plane through axes of symmetry or centres of holes.
Hatching should never be parallel or perpendicular to the main outline of the part.

formulas.plainText: Major axis of section of a cylinder = D / cos(theta)
True length along the cutting plane = top-view length / cos(theta)

notes.text: A half section suits symmetrical parts; it removes one quarter of the object and shows both interior and exterior in one view.
Do not hatch shafts, bolts, keys, ribs or spokes when the cutting plane passes along their length.
Revolved sections are drawn on the view itself, while removed sections are drawn away from the view and labelled.

formulas.title: Section ellipse of cylinder
formulas.plainText: Major axis = D / cos(theta), minor axis = D
formulas.description: True shape of the section of a vertical cylinder cut by a plane inclined at theta to HP.

formulas.title: True length on cutting plane
formulas.description: Recovers true lengths of the section from their foreshortened top-view lengths.

flashcards.front: At what angle are section lines normally drawn?
flashcards.back: At 45 degrees to the main outline or axis, as thin continuous evenly spaced lines.
A section taken with a stepped cutting plane so that it passes through features not lying in one straight line.

flashcards.front: How is a cutting-plane line drawn?
flashcards.back: As a thin chain line, thick at the ends and changes of direction, with arrows and letters showing viewing direction.

questions.questionText: Section lines (hatching) on a cut surface are normally drawn as:
questions.explanation: Hatching uses thin continuous evenly spaced lines, generally at 45 degrees to the outline or axis.

questions.questionText: A half section is most suitable for:
options: Symmetrical objects, showing interior and exterior in one view
Objects with holes not in a straight line
Showing a small local interior detail only
questions.explanation: A half section removes one quarter of a symmetrical object so that one half shows the interior and the other the exterior.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is normally hatched when the cutting plane passes along its axis in an assembly section?
questions.explanation: Shafts, bolts and ribs are conventionally left unsectioned when cut longitudinally; the hub body of a casting is hatched.

questions.questionText: A cross-section rotated through 90 degrees and superimposed on the view of an arm or spoke is called a:
questions.explanation: A revolved section is rotated in place on the view; a removed section is drawn outside the view.

questions.questionText: A vertical cylinder of 50 mm diameter is cut by a plane inclined at 60 degrees to HP. The major axis of the true shape of the section is:
questions.explanation: Major axis = D / cos 60 = 50 / 0.5 = 100 mm; the minor axis equals the diameter, 50 mm.
